tldr: This paper formulates the problem of a legged mobile manipulator actively selecting environmental support contacts (like walls or handrails). It proposes CTCS, an algorithm that uses local sensitivity analysis to cut computational cost by about two-thirds while rapidly finding the optimal contact surface and whole-body configuration.
hero_caption: An example of a legged mobile manipulator leveraging environmental contact. Under large external forces, the robot falls without support, but leaning a lateral plate against a wall or rail allows it to withstand disturbances stably. Available margins and ease of movement vary significantly depending on the chosen contact surface and posture.
overview:
Legged mobile manipulators—quadrupeds equipped with an arm—are expected to operate in rough terrain. However, when supporting heavy loads or reaching far, they can easily tip over due to self-weight and joint torque limits. Just as humans brace themselves against desks or walls, robots become much more stable when supported by nearby structures. However, bracing too firmly creates a trade-off: it restricts arm motion and prevents walking.

To address this, this study treats "which environmental contact surface to use and which whole-body configuration to adopt" jointly as decision variables. The authors define three capability metrics left over after satisfying task requirements: residual wrench, end-effector reach, and base mobility, balancing them against contact acquisition cost. However, evaluating these capabilities exactly by running whole-body optimizations over tens of thousands of candidates takes prohibitive time. The authors developed CTCS (Capability-Tradeoff Contact Selection), which clusters candidates with similar local geometry and contact Jacobians, and predicts surrounding capabilities from exact anchor evaluations using sensitivity analysis to prune the search space.

Evaluated across 392 simulation conditions and hardware experiments using a Unitree Go2 with a 7-DoF arm, selecting environmental contacts dramatically improved success rates and achieved capabilities compared to ground-only or fixed-contact baselines. Furthermore, CTCS demonstrated an approximately 3x speedup over exhaustive optimization while matching solution quality.
contributions: Formulated the joint selection of an environmental contact surface and whole-body configuration as a capability-tradeoff maximization problem balancing residual wrench, end-effector reach, and base mobility.
Developed CTCS, an algorithm that rapidly evaluates massive candidate sets by combining exact feasibility screening with local sensitivity-based capability predictions.
Demonstrated in simulations (392 conditions) and hardware experiments that CTCS outperforms fixed-contact and ground-only support while achieving roughly a 3x speedup over exhaustive optimization.

sections.heading: Leaning on a Wall: Treating Contact as a Decision Variable
sections.summary: To enable legged mobile manipulators to perform loco-manipulation tasks under heavy external forces, this paper proposes actively selecting environmental surfaces as auxiliary support. It models the trade-off between physical support and motion restriction via three capability measures, introducing the intuition behind CTCS for fast candidate evaluation.
sections.details:
Legged mobile manipulators must balance their bodies while executing tasks with their end-effectors. However, when large wrenches (forces and torques) act on the end-effector or when reaching far, they can easily lose balance. Just as a human rests a hand on a table to grab a distant object, a robot can withstand otherwise destabilizing loads by using walls or handrails as auxiliary support points.

Crucially, while an environmental contact provides physical support, it also constrains the robot's degrees of freedom. For instance, consider a robot walking while aiming a water cannon. It wants a strong wall contact to brace against the jet's recoil, but it still needs arm mobility to steer the stream, and excessive friction on the contact surface would prevent forward locomotion. In short, there is a clear trade-off in how contact is established.

This study adopts an approach that jointly selects the environmental contact surface and the whole-body configuration realizing that contact as decision variables. After satisfying task requirements, the remaining margins are quantified using three capability metrics: (1) residual wrench, (2) residual reach, and (3) residual base mobility.

However, solving this problem faces a steep computational hurdle. With countless potential surfaces and configurations, evaluating capabilities requires repeated whole-body optimizations for every candidate. To overcome this, the authors propose CTCS, combining exact feasibility screening with capability predictions via local sensitivity analysis.

captions.F1: Illustrations showing the effect of environmental support. (a) Without environmental support, the robot rolls and falls under external loads; (b) with support, it remains stable. Depending on the contact method, (c) patch contact or (d) edge contact yields different whole-body configurations and task capabilities.

sections.heading: How Does It Differ from Prior Work? From Planning to Selection
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work on whole-body support with environmental contact, contact planning, and fast candidate evaluation. Unlike conventional footstep planning or methods relying on predefined contacts, this work uniquely focuses on rapidly selecting the optimal persistent auxiliary contact for a given task.
sections.details:
### II-A Whole-Body Support with Environmental Contact
Conventional legged mobile manipulators rely primarily on foot ground-reaction forces for support. Prior work on humanoids and quadrupeds has explored bracing against walls to recover from disturbances or leaning on surfaces to surpass joint torque limits. However, most existing approaches assume the contact surface is predetermined. Because available forces and mobility change depending on how contact is made with the same surface, a framework is needed to actively choose the contact realization based on the task.

### II-B Contact Selection
In locomotion and manipulation planning, mixed-integer programming (MIP) and L1-norm relaxations (such as SL1M) are widely used to optimize terrain footstep sequences. However, these focus on contact sequence planning—determining how to sequence individual steps. In contrast, this paper addresses static contact selection for persistent loco-manipulation tasks: "which surface among multiple nearby options to choose, and which whole-body configuration to take." The granularity of the problem formulation is fundamentally different.

### II-C Efficient Evaluation of Contact Candidates
The search space across discrete surfaces and continuous whole-body postures is vast. While trajectory optimization combined with search or machine learning predictions has been explored, capability values change discontinuously when the contact surface changes or when active constraints (torque or friction limits) switch. Single global approximation models therefore tend to fail, creating a demand for efficient evaluation methods that preserve local structures.

sections.heading: Formulating Capability Trade-offs: Three Margins and the Optimization Problem
sections.summary: After defining robot dynamics and environmental contact conditions, the formulation introduces three capability metrics after meeting task requirements: residual wrench, residual reach, and residual base mobility. An optimization problem is framed to maximize a weighted utility function minus contact acquisition costs.
sections.details:
### III-A Modeling the Robot and Environmental Contact
The robot's whole-body configuration is denoted as $q=(p_b, R_b, q_\ell, q_m)$ (base position/orientation, leg joint angles, arm joint angles). An auxiliary support plate is attached to the robot's side. For an environmental surface $\Pi$, a contact point position constraint (C1) and a task-dependent contact mode (C2) are imposed. Contact modes include sticking (static contact with zero velocity) and sliding (moving with tangential velocity), governed by static and dynamic friction models, respectively.

### III-B Task Requirements and Three Capability Metrics
The task requirement (T1) demands satisfying the required end-effector wrench $w_e^d$, end-effector position $p_e^d$, and base velocity $v_b^d$ across all stance phases during locomotion (including two-legged phases in trotting). Beyond satisfying these, remaining margins are measured by three capability metrics:
- **Residual Wrench Capability ($\rho_{\rm wrench}^s$)**: How much additional disturbance wrench can be withstood while maintaining end-effector position and base velocity. Defined as the radius of the largest origin-centered Euclidean ball inside the convex hull of permissible residual wrenches along task coordinate axes.
- **Residual End-Effector Reach Capability ($\rho_{\rm reach}^s$)**: The radius representing how far the end-effector can move in each coordinate direction over a small time step $\tau$ while maintaining required wrench and base velocity.
- **Residual Base Mobility ($\rho_{\rm mob}^s$)**: The margin by which base velocity can increase or decrease along the heading direction during locomotion while maintaining required wrench and end-effector position.
These metrics are evaluated at their minimum (worst-case) across all stance phases $s$ to form the capability vector $\underline{\xi}(\chi)$.

### III-C Optimization Problem and Challenges
The objective function $J(\chi)$ is the weighted sum of the capability vector $\underline{\xi}(\chi)$ minus the acquisition cost $C_{\rm acq}$ from the initial configuration $q_0$. The goal is finding the surface-posture pair $\chi^*$ that maximizes $J(\chi)$ subject to constraints. However, evaluating a single candidate requires solving multiple linear programs (LPs), causing a computational explosion as candidate counts grow.

sections.heading: CTCS: Smart Pruning via Grouping and Sensitivity Analysis
sections.summary: The proposed CTCS method operates in five stages: (1) candidate generation and screening, (2) grouping and anchor selection, (3) prediction via sensitivity analysis, (4) verification, and (5) shortlisting and exact selection. Restricting expensive optimization to representative anchors yields massive speedups.
sections.details:
The CTCS pipeline proceeds through five stages:

### IV-A Candidate Generation and Feasibility Screening
For each environmental surface $\Pi$, arm joint angles, base pose, and foot placements are sampled to produce candidate configurations satisfying kinematics and contact constraints (C1, C2). Next, task requirements (T1) are checked across all stance phases, retaining only feasible candidates $\mathcal{D}_1$. This screening step is computationally fast.

### IV-B Grouping and Anchor Selection
Evaluating capabilities exactly for all surviving candidates in $\mathcal{D}_1$ is still too slow. Thus, candidates on the same surface with similar whole-body coordinates $\theta$ and contact Jacobians $J_c(q)$ are clustered into groups using complete-linkage clustering. Including the contact Jacobian ensures grouping candidates that share similar contact force impacts on the body and similar motion constraint geometries.
Candidates closest to each group's center are evaluated exactly in order; the first candidate meeting two criteria is designated as an anchor:
- (R1) Non-degenerate optimal basis in directional LPs (ensuring a stable basis and uniquely defined sensitivity analysis).
- (R2) Directional capability margins exceeding a positive threshold (avoiding near-zero numerical instabilities).

### IV-C Anchor-Based Prediction, Verification, and Final Selection
Using the gradient of the Lagrangian at anchor $\hat{\chi}$'s optimal solution and the implicit function theorem, capability shifts around the anchor are predicted via first-order approximation (local sensitivity analysis):
$$\widetilde{\mathcal{V}}_{p,s}(\chi_i) = \mathcal{V}_{p,s}(\hat{\chi}) + \nabla_\theta \mathcal{V}_{p,s}(\hat{\chi})^\top (\theta_i - \hat{\theta})$$
This allows immediate estimation of each candidate's capability $\hat{\underline{\xi}}(\chi_i)$.
To catch model breakdowns, two-fold verification is performed: (i) a probe test evaluating the farthest group member to check prediction error (splitting the group in half if it fails), and (ii) cross-anchor checks comparing predictions against overlapping anchors. Inconsistent candidates are sent for exact evaluation.
Finally, the top $N_{\rm short}$ candidates ranked by predicted score $\widehat{J}(\chi)$ form a shortlist $\mathcal{D}_{\rm short}$. Only these shortlisted candidates undergo exact evaluation to select the best final candidate.

captions.F2: Overview of the CTCS algorithm. Candidates are grouped, central anchors (yellow stars) are selected, and surrounding capabilities are predicted via sensitivity analysis. After probe tests and cross-checks, promising candidates (double circles) are evaluated exactly to determine the final solution (purple star).

sections.heading: Simulation and Hardware Validation: 3x Faster than Exhaustive, Vastly Better than Fixed Contact
sections.summary: Evaluations across 9 support surfaces and 392 task conditions in Gazebo and on hardware with a Unitree Go2 and arm showed CTCS matches exhaustive search quality while running over 3x faster. Hardware tests verified stable locomotion and load resistance while maintaining sliding contact.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Baselines
The platform consisted of a Unitree Go2 with a lateral support plate and a mounted 7-DoF AgileX NERO arm. The environment contained nine 5m-long support surfaces: one wall, four tables of varying heights, and four handrails of varying heights. Testing covered 392 conditions spanning 14 wrench directions and 14 force magnitudes (5–70N) across sticking and walking modes (trot gait, base velocity 0.1m/s).
Baselines included "Exhaustive" (exact evaluation of all candidates), "Ground-only" (no environmental contact), and "Fixed-Contact" (a single predetermined contact pose).

### V-A & V-B Contact Quality and Computation Time
In Gazebo simulations under sticking mode, the task certification rate (finding a feasible solution) reached 91.8% for CTCS compared to 68.4% for Ground-only. The mean objective value rose significantly from 2.5324 to 3.5419. Conversely, Fixed-Contact certified only 48.5%, performing worse than Ground-only. This highlights that contact hinders performance if not chosen to suit the task.
Computationally, Exhaustive required 124.0s (sticking) and 157.0s (walking), whereas CTCS took 39.1s and 62.1s—speedups of roughly 3.17x and 2.53x, respectively. The resulting objective values closely matched Exhaustive (100% match in walking mode), proving candidate pruning did not degrade solution quality.
Ablations without verification ("CTCS-NV") or with single anchors per surface ("CTCS-SA") suffered degraded objective values, confirming the necessity of grouping and verification.

### V-C Surface Selection Trends by Task
Surface selection showed intuitive patterns. In walking mode, handrails were selected 78.9% of the time, while the wall was chosen only 3.9%. Rails have a lower dynamic friction coefficient in the model, minimizing resistance while sliding during forward locomotion. In sticking mode, the wall's selection rate rose to 17.8% due to its bracing capacity. Selection rates also varied among rails of different heights, demonstrating that choices account for both geometry and friction.

### V-D Hardware Experiments
Physical experiments tested static vertical load resistance (approx. 19N) and sliding-contact locomotion. Without environmental contact, the robot collapsed under arm and load weight; with CTCS-selected support, it performed tasks stably. During walking, it tracked commanded velocities while keeping end-effector tracking errors mostly below 30mm despite trotting impact oscillations.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Outlook
sections.summary: The experiments demonstrated the effectiveness of CTCS in jointly selecting contact surfaces and whole-body configurations. Because the current approach relies on discrete sampling, future work targets continuous global optimization and online contact transitions.
sections.details:
This paper presented CTCS, a capability-tradeoff contact selection method for legged mobile manipulators. It verified the necessity of treating environmental contact as an optimization decision variable tailored to the task, rather than a fixed assumption. The proposed method substantially cut computation time while matching exhaustive evaluation quality, demonstrating high disturbance resistance and tracking performance on hardware.

The authors identified three primary limitations and future research avenues:
- Since candidate generation relies on sampling, global optimality in continuous space is not theoretically guaranteed (continuous candidate refinement is needed).
- Dynamic contact transitions—switching across different surfaces on the fly—are not supported.
- Real-time online replanning to re-select contacts when task requirements change abruptly during operation.

takeaways: Environmental contact carries a fundamental trade-off between increasing support and restricting mobility; active selection tailored to task requirements (force, reach, velocity) is essential.

In search problems requiring numerous whole-body optimizations, local clustering via posture coordinates and contact Jacobians combined with sensitivity-based linear prediction dramatically cuts computational cost.
Optimal contact surfaces vary significantly with task dynamics; for instance, low-friction handrails are preferred when walking while maintaining sliding contact.
limitations: Because posture generation relies on sampling, there is no theoretical guarantee of finding the true global optimum in continuous space.
While computation is about 3x faster (30–60 seconds), it remains too slow for full online, real-time replanning.
The method does not support dynamic multi-contact transition planning across multiple consecutive surfaces.
